name: Salvador Dalí Museum
overview: Museum of the work of Salvador Dalí at One Dali Blvd on the downtown waterfront of St. Petersburg, Florida; it calls itself The Dalí.
Built on the collection of Reynolds and Eleanor Morse, who began buying Dalí's work in 1942 and opened a first museum in Beachwood, Ohio in March 1971.
The collection moved to a renovated marine warehouse in St. Petersburg, which opened on 7 March 1982.
funding_verdict: Salvador Dalí Museum: self-earning nonprofit: ticket and programme income, with tourist tax money for its expansion

name: Philbrook Museum of Art
overview: An art museum in the Villa Philbrook and its gardens at 2727 S Rockford Rd, Tulsa (museum website).

Waite and Genevieve Phillips established the museum by donating their residence to the community in 1938; it opened on 25 October 1939 under its first director, Eugene Kingman, and took the name The Philbrook Museum of Art in 1987 (Oklahoma Historical Society).

What is there: the collection began with a few works from the Tulsa Art Association and the villa's furnishings and grew mainly by gift. Native American art has been a major part since the early years: pottery and basketry from Clark Field from 1942, the Roberta Campbell Lawson collection in 1947, University of Tulsa collections transferred to the museum, and the Indian Annual, 1946 to 1979. Other holdings include European and American paintings from Laura A. Clubb (1947), Italian Renaissance works from the Samuel H. Kress Foundation (1961), and Asian, African and antiquities collections (Oklahoma Historical Society). The pages read did not give an object count.
funding_verdict: Philbrook Museum of Art: private, mainly foundation and individual gifts, with state and federal arts grants

name: Munson-Williams-Proctor Arts Institute
overview: An art museum, performing arts centre and art school at 310 Genesee Street, Utica, New York, with a gallery building by Philip Johnson and the Victorian Italianate mansion Fountain Elms (museum website, History).

Founded in 1919, with the concept drafted after 1915 by Maria Williams Proctor, her husband Thomas R. Proctor and her brother-in-law Frederick Proctor, and opened in May 1936; it was updated to the name Munson in 2023 (museum website, History).

What is there: Hudson River School landscapes by Frederic Church, Asher B. Durand and Martin Johnson Heade, Thomas Cole's four-part The Voyage of Life painted in 1839 and 1840, and still lifes by Raphael Peale, John Peto and others (museum website, Highlights from the Collection). Fountain Elms holds period rooms.
funding_verdict: Munson-Williams-Proctor Arts Institute: mainly earned income from classes and programmes, plus investments, gifts and a state arts grant

name: Folger Shakespeare Library
overview: Research library, museum and theatre at 201 East Capitol Street SE on Capitol Hill (Folger website).
Opened in 1932 as a gift to the American people from Henry and Emily Folger, who made their first rare book purchase in 1889 (Folger website).

Holds more than 300,000 objects, which the Folger calls the world's largest Shakespeare collection, with books, manuscripts and prints from the 1500s to the early 1700s; all 82 of its First Folios are shown in a 20-foot "visible vault" (Folger website; FY24 annual report).
funding_verdict: Folger Shakespeare Library: endowed: the Folgers' bequest, managed by Amherst College's trustees, with private gifts

name: National Museum of Women in the Arts
overview: Private, nonprofit museum of art by women at 1250 New York Ave. NW in downtown Washington, DC.
Founded by Wilhelmina Cole Holladay and Wallace F. Holladay and incorporated in November 1981; it opened in its building in April 1987.
The Holladay Collection, begun in the 1970s, is the core of the holdings.
funding_verdict: National Museum of Women in the Arts: privately funded: members, individual donors, endowment income and earned income

name: Norton Museum of Art
aliases: Norton Gallery and School of Art
overview: An art museum at 1450 S. Dixie Highway in West Palm Beach, in a 1941 Art Deco building by Marion Sims Wyeth extended by Foster + Partners (museum website).

Founded by Ralph Hubbard Norton (1875 to 1953), an industrialist who headed the Acme Steel Company in Chicago, and his wife Elizabeth Calhoun Norton (1881 to 1947); it opened to the public on 8 February 1941 as the Norton Gallery and School of Art (museum website).

The collection holds more than 8,900 works in five departments, European, American, Asian, Contemporary and Photography; the Nortons' gifts form its core, and later purchases include Stuart Davis's New York Mural, acquired in 1964, and a Jackson Pollock acquired in 1971 (museum website).
funding_verdict: Norton Museum of Art: private, about seven tenths from contributions

name: Clark Art Institute
aliases: Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute
overview: An art museum in Williamstown, Massachusetts, whose campus includes the Museum Building and the Manton Research Center, joined by a 1973 addition designed by Pietro Belluschi and The Architects Collaborative (iBerkshires, 28 October 2024).
The director is Olivier Meslay, Hardymon Director; Esther Bell is deputy director and Robert and Martha Berman Lipp Chief Curator (iBerkshires, 28 October 2024).

In October 2024 the collection gained 331 works from the Aso O. Tavitian Foundation: 132 paintings, 130 sculptures, 39 drawings and 30 decorative arts objects, with works by Bernini, Andrea della Robbia, Jan van Eyck, Vigée Le Brun, Parmigianino, Rubens, Jacques-Louis David and Gil de Siloé (The Art Newspaper, 28 October 2024).
funding_verdict: Clark Art Institute: private, funded by gifts and its own assets; one foundation gift of more than $45m dominates recent income

name: Worcester Art Museum
overview: A museum of art at 55 Salisbury Street, Worcester, Massachusetts, in a historic campus now being renovated in more than 130 capital projects (museum website, campus transformation page).

Stephen Salisbury III gave land and $100,000 for construction and endowment, other citizens gave the rest, ground was broken on 18 March 1897 and the museum opened on 10 May 1898 (museum website, history page).

What is there: nearly 40,000 objects in American art, arms and armor, Asian art, European art, post-modern and contemporary art, ancient art, and prints, drawings and photographs (museum website). Early holdings included Gilbert Stuart portraits, Paul Revere silver and, as the museum puts it, America's first public collection of Japanese prints; a 12th century Romanesque chapter house from France was bought in 1927, and The Last Judgement tapestry in 1935 (museum website, history page).
funding_verdict: Worcester Art Museum: mainly private, through donors, a foundation gift record and an endowment of about $110 million

name: 32° East | Ugandan Arts Trust
overview: Independent non-profit and home for the visual arts community in Uganda, at Plot 212 Sonko Close, Kabalagala, Kampala, behind Equity Bank (stated by the trust).

Founded in 2011. Myriad USA's 2022 article names the founders as the British nationals Rocca Holly-Nambi and Nikki Elphinstone, and The Skinny (2013) names them as Rocca Gutteridge and Nicola Elphinstone. Teesa Bahana is now director.
Operated from metal shipping containers for years, then bought a plot off Ggaba Road and built a permanent centre (Myriad USA, 2022).
funding_verdict: 32° East | Ugandan Arts Trust: foundation-funded and crowd-funded: Sigrid Rausing Trust and other European and US funders, plus individual donors

press_items.title: Kalanzi Kajubi, "32° East is a Sanctuary for Visual Arts in Uganda" (9 May 2025)
Rosamund West, "32º East: Art of Africa" (3 December 2013)

name: Musée National des Beaux-Arts d'Alger
overview: National museum of fine arts on the wooded hill of the Hamma district of Algiers, facing the Bay of Algiers and the Jardin d'Essai; Algerian state media now call it the Musée public national des Beaux-Arts (museum website, Radio Algérienne).

It took over the collection of the Algiers municipal museum, which opened in a former barracks on 30 May 1908 and closed in 1928; the new museum was inaugurated on 5 May 1930 and opened to the public in April 1931, as one of the projects of the centenary of French Algeria (Wikipedia, French Wikipedia).

Building: designed by Paul Guion and begun in 1928, with furniture by Louis Fernez; the museum gives more than 4,000 square metres of built space, as much again in gardens, and three exhibition levels (Wikipedia, museum website).
funding_verdict: Musée National des Beaux-Arts d'Alger: public: the Algerian state, through the Ministry of Culture and Arts

name: National Gallery of Armenia
overview: National art museum on Republic Square in Yerevan, in the building it shares with the History Museum of Armenia (Wikipedia, Republic Square article).

Founded in 1921 under a decree of the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic as the artistic section of the state museum. Its core came from the collection of the Armenian Cultural Center (the former Lazarian Seminary in Moscow) and gifts from Armenian artists. By 1925 about 400 works hung in six halls (Wikipedia).
It became a separate art museum in 1935, was renamed the State Picture Gallery of Armenia in 1947 and became the National Gallery of Armenia in 1991 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: National Gallery of Armenia: run by the Armenian government, with the Ministry of Culture involved in staffing and a government programme for a new building

press_items.title: "Collection of National Gallery of Armenia in poor conditions" (17 January 2017, no author named)
"Staff Changes at National Picture Gallery" (3 February 2011, no author named)

name: Samstag Museum of Art
overview: University art museum in the Hawke Building at 55 North Terrace, Adelaide, on the corner of Fenn Place and North Terrace (the museum's website). It describes itself as South Australia's largest contemporary art gallery (stated by the museum).

Opened on 11 October 2007 with the exhibition "Wonderful World". Its roots are the College Gallery of about 1977 at the Underdale campus. It became the University of South Australia Art Museum in 1991 and moved to the City West campus in 1998.
In 2007 it was renamed the Anne & Gordon Samstag Museum of Art.
funding_verdict: Samstag Museum of Art (Adelaide): part of Adelaide University, with a private bequest funding its scholarships

name: Murray Art Museum Albury
overview: Contemporary art museum, known as MAMA, at 546 Dean Street, Albury, New South Wales (museum website).
It grew out of the Albury Regional Art Gallery and opened on 2 October 2015 with "Wiradjuri Ngurambanggu (On Wiradjuri Country)", works by contemporary Indigenous artists (Wikipedia).

Building: a $10.5 million refurbishment renovated the former gallery and the neighbouring Burrows House, with extensions linking both into QEII Square, designed by NBRS and Partners. Floor space grew from 832 m2 to 2,036 m2 and the building has seven galleries over two levels (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Murray Art Museum Albury: mainly public: AlburyCity Council and Create NSW, with philanthropic benefactors

name: Art Gallery of Ballarat
overview: Municipal art gallery at 40 Lydiard Street North, Ballarat, Victoria, on Wadawurrung Country. The gallery website says the building is closed for building upgrades, including the gallery shop, and directs visitors to Backspace Gallery at 43 Mair Street.

Opened on 11 September 1884 as the Ballarat Fine Art Gallery in rented space at the Ballarat Academy of Music, opened by Governor Henry Loch. The benefactor James Oddie is described as its "patron and founder", and a public association was formed in 1886 (Wikipedia). The word "fine" was dropped from the name in 2008 (Wikipedia).

Building: Renaissance Revival, designed by Tappin, Gilbert and Dennehy, built from 1887 to 1890 and opened by Alfred Deakin in 1890. Extended in 1927, 1987 and 2001 and restored in 2009 and 2022 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Art Gallery of Ballarat: mainly public: City of Ballarat, with Victorian Government grants and charitable foundations

press_items.title: Louise Tegart, gallery director, "OPINION: In defence of the Art Gallery" (25 January 2022)
Louis Alexander, reader letter, "Gallery director is a critical role for the future" (3 November 2017)

name: Bendigo Art Gallery
overview: Regional public gallery at 42 View Street, Bendigo, Victoria, owned and managed by the City of Greater Bendigo (Wikipedia; Art Collector).

Founded in 1887. The collection was first housed in the former Bendigo Volunteer Rifles room, which William Charles Vahland converted in 1890 into Bolton Court. William Beebe designed Drury Court in 1897 (Wikipedia).
Fender Katsalidis Architects designed a new sculpture gallery in a refurbishment and expansion from 1998 to 2001 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Bendigo Art Gallery: mainly public: City of Greater Bendigo and Victorian Government, with philanthropic foundations

name: Geelong Gallery
overview: Regional public art gallery on Little Malop Street in Johnstone Park, Geelong, about a three-minute walk from Geelong Railway Station (stated by the gallery).
Geelong Progress League members petitioned for a gallery in 1895. It opened on 31 May 1900 in the Geelong City Hall as Geelong Art Gallery (Wikipedia).
The current building opened in 1915 as a memorial to George M. Hitchcock and was extended in 1928, 1937, 1938, 1956 and 1971 and renovated in 2001 and 2017 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Geelong Gallery: grant-funded: grant income of A$1.67 million of A$2.85 million revenue, with the City of Greater Geelong and the Victorian Government named as partners, plus philanthropic foundations and individual donors

name: Blak Dot Gallery
overview: First Nations artist-run gallery at 33 Saxon Street, Brunswick, in Naarm (Melbourne), reached by Dawson Street. It describes itself as "Australia's leading gallery for contemporary First Nations art".
Founded in 2011 as an artist-run space. Its 2014 address was 413 Lygon Street, East Brunswick (TextaQueen), and it moved to its current premises behind the Brunswick baths in 2016 (Time Out).
Director Kimba Thompson leads the gallery with help from volunteers and artists (Time Out). It is a non-profit governed by a board.
funding_verdict: Blak Dot Gallery: mainly public: Australian Government, Victorian Government and Merri-bek Council grants

name: Potter Museum of Art
overview: University art museum on the University of Melbourne campus in Parkville, at the corner of Swanston Street and Masson Road. It is part of University of Melbourne Museums and Collections (Wikipedia; museum site).
It traces its origins to the University Gallery, established in 1972, and was renamed the Ian Potter Museum of Art in July 1998 when the current building opened (Wikipedia).
The 1998 building was designed by Katsalidis Architects and won a commendation for Public Architecture at the 1999 Australian Institute of Architects National Architecture Awards (ArchitectureAU).
funding_verdict: Potter Museum of Art: university museum: part of the University of Melbourne, with private donors and arts agencies named for the 2025 reopening
wider_context: Green Left (Jacob Andrewartha, "Student encampment forces Uni of Melbourne to disclose weapons ties", 23 May 2024) reported that after a four-week Gaza solidarity encampment and a week-long occupation the University of Melbourne agreed to disclose its funding arrangements with weapons corporations, that Unimelb for Palestine expected disclosure of ties to all weapons manufacturers including Lockheed Martin, Boeing and BAE Systems, and that the university rejected the demand to divest.

The Melburnian (Georgie Atkins, "University commits to disclose ties to weapons companies amid student protest", 28 May 2024) reported that the university committed to additional disclosure of its research grant arrangements, and named the same three companies.
Neither article names the Potter; the connection is that the Potter is part of the University of Melbourne (museum site).

press_items.title: Tim Stone, "The Big Review | 65,000 Years: A Short History of Australian Art at the Potter Museum of Art, Melbourne" (1 September 2025)

name: Shepparton Art Museum
overview: Art museum at 530 Wyndham Street, Shepparton, Victoria (Shepparton Art Museum).
Established in 1936 as the Shepparton Art Gallery, a council gallery. The collection had no purpose-built home until the current building opened in November 2021 (Wikipedia).
Denton Corker Marshall won the 2017 design competition. Construction began in 2019. The building cost $50 million and won the 2022 Victorian Architecture Award for Public Architecture (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Shepparton Art Museum: Greater Shepparton City Council and Creative Victoria, with named donors and the SAM Foundation

name: Artbank
overview: Australian Government art-leasing programme that buys works from living Australian artists and leases them to businesses, government agencies and individuals. Collection stores are in Sydney, Melbourne and Perth (Wikipedia).

Established by the Australian Government in 1980, modelled on Canada's Art Bank. Arts minister Bob Ellicott saw the Ottawa collection in 1979 and persuaded Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser. The Treasurer, John Howard, approved A$250,000 in seed funding (Wikipedia).
The collection began with 600 works from the National Gallery of Australia (Wikipedia). It had grown to 10,950 works by the time of the 2023 audit (Government News).
funding_verdict: Artbank: self-funded by leasing income, inside a federal department
wider_context: In April 2023 the Australian National Audit Office (Auditor-General Grant Hehir) found that the department's handling of Artbank "has not been appropriate" (Government News, Canberra Times).

Acquisitions did not follow the Commonwealth Procurement Rules and skipped open or competitive processes; value for money was not documented or demonstrated, and public reporting was limited (Region Canberra, Canberra Times).

About 40% of the collection was leased against a target of 70%; 30% was never leased from July 2015 to June 2022 and a further 29% was leased for less than half the time it was available (Government News, Region Canberra, Canberra Times).
Approvals for removing over 70 works were obtained after the fact, though the works had been sold more than four years earlier (Region Canberra).

Acquisition spending fell from A$507,993 for 179 works in 2016 to 2017 to A$396,462 for 75 works in 2021 to 2022; applications to the artist pitch roadshows fell from 40 in 2016 to three in 2021 (Government News).

The department defended its approach by citing a rule allowing "limited tender". Its secretary, Jim Betts, wrote that he was "concerned that aspects of the narrative may unduly and adversely impact the reputation and operation of Artbank" (Canberra Times).
